## What it is

The name comes from a post on the overrepresentation of small states. Wyoming has 0.2% of the U.S. population and 2% of the senators, and "the 21 smallest states have the population of California but 42 Senators compared to California's two"; Gelman and his colleagues found similar small-state advantages in representation and spending in other countries. One reason such inequality persists, he suggests, is that it isn't recognized: "in many contexts, the states are presented as equals. For example, USA Today has a feature with news from each of the 50 states. There are a lot more people in Los Angeles or Chicago than in several of the smallest states, but they manage to find an equal-length snippet from each."

More generally, a summary or graph that treats every state, country or district as one unit commits the USA Today fallacy when the question is really about *people*. *Thirty states saw an increase* says nothing about how many Americans saw one. On a map, Montana takes up much more ink than New Jersey, though New Jersey has about eight times as many residents.

## Why it matters

Averages over jurisdictions and averages over people answer different questions, and they can differ a lot when the outcome is correlated with population size. Urban–rural differences make this common: large states are more urban. A state-level average can tell the opposite story from the population average. Choropleth maps make it worse by giving visual weight according to land area.

## How it works

If $\theta_s$ is the value in state $s$ and $N_s$ its population,

$$
\bar\theta_{\text{states}} = \frac{1}{S}\sum_s \theta_s
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
\bar\theta_{\text{people}} = \frac{\sum_s N_s\,\theta_s}{\sum_s N_s}.
$$

The two agree only if $\theta_s$ is uncorrelated with $N_s$. Decide which one answers your question. If it's about people, weight by population, and size your graphical elements accordingly.

## Simulated example

The populations below are approximate 2020 census figures. The outcome is simulated so that it is correlated with state size, as many urban–rural outcomes are. Compare the unweighted state average with the population-weighted one.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, sum, mean, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof sizeCorr = Inputs.range([-10, 10], {value: 6, step: 0.5, label: "How much the outcome rises with log population"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 15, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
pops = ({"California":39.5,"Texas":29.1,"Florida":21.5,"New York":20.2,"Pennsylvania":13.0,"Illinois":12.8,"Ohio":11.8,"Georgia":10.7,"North Carolina":10.4,"Michigan":10.1,"New Jersey":9.3,"Virginia":8.6,"Washington":7.7,"Arizona":7.2,"Massachusetts":7.0,"Tennessee":6.9,"Indiana":6.8,"Maryland":6.2,"Missouri":6.2,"Wisconsin":5.9,"Colorado":5.8,"Minnesota":5.7,"South Carolina":5.1,"Alabama":5.0,"Louisiana":4.7,"Kentucky":4.5,"Oregon":4.2,"Oklahoma":4.0,"Connecticut":3.6,"Utah":3.3,"Iowa":3.2,"Nevada":3.1,"Arkansas":3.0,"Mississippi":3.0,"Kansas":2.9,"New Mexico":2.1,"Nebraska":2.0,"Idaho":1.8,"West Virginia":1.8,"Hawaii":1.5,"New Hampshire":1.4,"Maine":1.4,"Rhode Island":1.1,"Montana":1.1,"Delaware":1.0,"South Dakota":0.9,"North Dakota":0.8,"Alaska":0.7,"Vermont":0.6,"Wyoming":0.6})
```

```{ojs}
usa = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const entries = Object.entries(pops);
  const lm = mean(entries.map(([, p]) => Math.log(p)));
  return entries.map(([state, pop]) => ({state, pop, value: 50 + sizeCorr * (Math.log(pop) - lm) + r.normal(0, 4)}));
}
summary = ({
  states: mean(usa.map(d => d.value)),
  people: sum(usa.map(d => d.value * d.pop)) / sum(usa.map(d => d.pop))
})
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "The USA Today Fallacy: simulation chart",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: State population (millions, log scale). Vertical axis: Outcome. The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",
  height: 320,
  x: {label: "State population (millions, log scale)", type: "log", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Outcome", grid: true},
  r: {range: [2, 22]},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(usa, {x: "pop", y: "value", r: "pop", fill: "#2166ac", fillOpacity: 0.35, stroke: "#2166ac", title: "state"}),
    Plot.text(usa.filter(d => d.pop > 15 || d.pop < 0.8), {x: "pop", y: "value", text: "state", dy: -12, fontSize: 10}),
    Plot.ruleY([summary.states], {stroke: "#d6604d", strokeDasharray: "5 3"}),
    Plot.ruleY([summary.people], {stroke: "currentColor"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`Average across the 50 states (dashed red): **${fmt(summary.states, 1)}**. Average across *people* (solid line): **${fmt(summary.people, 1)}**. The four largest states hold about a third of the population, and an unweighted state average gives them 4 votes out of 50.`}</div>`
```

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# The USA Today Fallacy: averaging over states is not averaging over people.
size_corr <- 6 # how much the outcome rises with log population # <1>
set.seed(15) # <2>

pop <- c( # <3>
  California = 39.5, Texas = 29.1, Florida = 21.5,
  "New York" = 20.2, Pennsylvania = 13.0, Illinois = 12.8,
  Ohio = 11.8, Georgia = 10.7, "North Carolina" = 10.4,
  Michigan = 10.1, "New Jersey" = 9.3, Virginia = 8.6,
  Washington = 7.7, Arizona = 7.2, Massachusetts = 7.0,
  Tennessee = 6.9, Indiana = 6.8, Maryland = 6.2, Missouri = 6.2,
  Wisconsin = 5.9, Colorado = 5.8, Minnesota = 5.7,
  "South Carolina" = 5.1, Alabama = 5.0, Louisiana = 4.7,
  Kentucky = 4.5, Oregon = 4.2, Oklahoma = 4.0, Connecticut = 3.6,
  Utah = 3.3, Iowa = 3.2, Nevada = 3.1, Arkansas = 3.0,
  Mississippi = 3.0, Kansas = 2.9, "New Mexico" = 2.1,
  Nebraska = 2.0, Idaho = 1.8, "West Virginia" = 1.8, Hawaii = 1.5,
  "New Hampshire" = 1.4, Maine = 1.4, "Rhode Island" = 1.1,
  Montana = 1.1, Delaware = 1.0, "South Dakota" = 0.9,
  "North Dakota" = 0.8, Alaska = 0.7, Vermont = 0.6, Wyoming = 0.6
)
value <- 50 + size_corr * (log(pop) - mean(log(pop))) + rnorm(50, 0, 4) # <4>
cat("Average across the 50 states: ", round(mean(value), 1),
  "\nAverage across people: ", round(weighted.mean(value, pop), 1),
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)

plot(pop, value, # <5>
  log = "x", pch = 19, cex = sqrt(pop) / 2,
  col = adjustcolor("#2166ac", 0.6),
  xlab = "Population (millions)", ylab = "Outcome"
)
abline(h = mean(value), col = "#d6604d", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(h = weighted.mean(value, pop), lwd = 2)
```
1. The page's control: how much the outcome rises with a state's population.
2. Fixes the random numbers so the run is reproducible.
3. Approximate 2020 populations of the 50 states, in millions.
4. A simulated outcome correlated with state size, as many urban-rural outcomes are.
5. The outcome against population, dots sized by population. The dashed line averages over states, the solid line over people, and they differ because the big states are different.

## Python {.unlisted}

```{.python}
# The USA Today Fallacy: averaging over states is not averaging over people.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

size_corr = 6  # how much the outcome rises with log population
rng = np.random.default_rng(15)

pop = {"California": 39.5, "Texas": 29.1, "Florida": 21.5,
       "New York": 20.2, "Pennsylvania": 13.0, "Illinois": 12.8,
       "Ohio": 11.8, "Georgia": 10.7, "North Carolina": 10.4,
       "Michigan": 10.1, "New Jersey": 9.3, "Virginia": 8.6,
       "Washington": 7.7, "Arizona": 7.2, "Massachusetts": 7.0,
       "Tennessee": 6.9, "Indiana": 6.8, "Maryland": 6.2, "Missouri": 6.2,
       "Wisconsin": 5.9, "Colorado": 5.8, "Minnesota": 5.7,
       "South Carolina": 5.1, "Alabama": 5.0, "Louisiana": 4.7,
       "Kentucky": 4.5, "Oregon": 4.2, "Oklahoma": 4.0, "Connecticut": 3.6,
       "Utah": 3.3, "Iowa": 3.2, "Nevada": 3.1, "Arkansas": 3.0,
       "Mississippi": 3.0, "Kansas": 2.9, "New Mexico": 2.1,
       "Nebraska": 2.0, "Idaho": 1.8, "West Virginia": 1.8, "Hawaii": 1.5,
       "New Hampshire": 1.4, "Maine": 1.4, "Rhode Island": 1.1,
       "Montana": 1.1, "Delaware": 1.0, "South Dakota": 0.9,
       "North Dakota": 0.8, "Alaska": 0.7, "Vermont": 0.6, "Wyoming": 0.6}
p = np.array(list(pop.values()))
value = (50 + size_corr * (np.log(p) - np.log(p).mean())
         + rng.normal(0, 4, 50))
print(f"Average across the 50 states: {value.mean():.1f}")
print(f"Average across people: {np.average(value, weights=p):.1f}")

plt.scatter(p, value, s=10 * p, color="#2166ac", alpha=0.6)
plt.xscale("log")
plt.axhline(value.mean(), color="#d6604d", linestyle="--", linewidth=2,
            label="Average of states")
plt.axhline(np.average(value, weights=p), color="black", linewidth=2,
            label="Average of people")
plt.xlabel("Population (millions)")
plt.ylabel("Outcome")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Decide whether your unit of analysis is the jurisdiction or the person.
- When outcomes correlate with size, state-weighted and population-weighted summaries can disagree a lot.
- On maps, land area is not population. Consider cartograms or population-sized symbols.
:::
